rationale: INCOMING_RUST. `overrides` was RULED on prose — 'Rust trait impls are captured as implements' — and the ontology gate exists because a prose justification survived a whole wave and was wrong: the lane's corpus measurement found 252 `implements` edges over 44 files of ripgrep plus 107 in-file trait-implementation sites, so the construct is common and the language states it. Rust has no `override` keyword: `impl Trait for Type { fn m() }` REPLACES the trait's `m` for that type, and the author's writing of both ends IS the assertion, so nothing is inferred. (1) The two confidence tiers are the contract, not a detail: `local-trait-signature` at 1.0 means both ends are facts read out of THIS file (pinned on TWO traits, `Local` and `Foreign`, so a rule that only handled the first trait in a file would fail rather than pass), `cross-file-trait-signature` at 0.85 means the trait is not declared here and the target joins only once the whole project is indexed — a thresholded consumer must not treat it as ground truth. `Drop::drop` and `Read::read` are both pinned because they are the shapes a real corpus is made of, and `Read` is the one that proves the 0.85 tier is reachable rather than dead. (2) The negative half decides whether the label means anything: `only_in_impl` is a method `Local` does NOT declare, so the impl ADDS one and publishing `overrides` for it would put the label on an edge that is not an override. (3) An INHERENT impl (`impl Widget { fn inherent }`) publishes nothing — there is no trait, so nothing is displaced. This is the half a name-based rule gets wrong, and the R10/D30 precedent is that a rule which cannot see the `for` clause invents edges. (4) A QUALIFIED trait reference (`std::fmt::Display`) targets the LEAF `Display`, matching the lane's own `implements` leaf-target contract (#419-B) and the family's name-surface rule: a path prefix is not a dependency, the type is. (5) `implements` rows are pinned at confidenceMin 1 here because the lane measured 252 of 252 with NO confidence field at all — the absence was invisible from inside the analyzer because classifyEvidenceTier defaults a missing value to 1. (6) The `calls` confidence pin is here rather than in the payload fixture for a reason this file can show: the pre-round edge published NO confidence at all (17,083 of 17,083 rows on this lane's corpus), `classifyEvidenceTier` defaults a missing value to 1 so the evidence tier read correct, and no fixture asserted the field — so removing it passed every gate in the repository. A `confidenceMin` pin on ONE `calls` row is the whole fix and costs one line. (7) Two `calls` confidence pins, one per emission site: a `call_expression` callee and a `macro_invocation` name are separate emission sites with separate `confidence` fields, and a single pin covered whichever one the mutant did not touch — the first version of the lane mutant dropped the call-expression field and SURVIVED, which is the fixture-gap report the honesty contract asks for rather than a reason to weaken the pin. SUPERSESSION (2026-10-19, Lead decision §21.11 + task-9): this fixture previously carried TWO forbids that contradicted its own expects — `{target:'handle'}` and `{source:'Widget.handle',target:'handle'}` both match the CORRECT owner-qualified override row the expects require, so the fixture could never pass and the forbid was pinning the wrong shape. Resolved IN FAVOUR OF THE EXPECT (the trait-override contract wins; the same decision makes foreign/cross-file overrides real relationships). Coverage is not weakened: the two stale forbids are REPLACED by the shapes they were trying to describe — a BARE method name as the source (a method leaf does not say WHICH type's) and the REVERSED direction (trait/source -> implementing type).
